subject: mathematics
question_text: Show that the determinant with rows (1, a, a²), (1, b, b²) and (1, c, c²) is (a−b)(b−c)(c−a).

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), book p.39, chapter 5 MATRICES, Short Answer question 4. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. ⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The 1+1+1+1 shape gives one mark to each of the four moves: the row subtractions, the two common factors, the expansion, and the last factor. Paper position: Maths-1A Section B runs Q11 to Q18 at 4 marks each, answer any 6 of 8, under the 2026-27 pattern; Matrices carries a Section B slot and also appears in Section C. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this one — name each row operation in order.

steps.label: Subtract the rows in pairs
steps.margin_note: First mark. Do not expand this determinant. Subtracting neighbouring rows is what creates the differences a−b and b−c that the answer is built from.
steps.memory_tip: Subtract neighbouring rows first — that is what makes the factors a−b and b−c appear.
lines: Let Δ be the given determinant:

lines.text: \Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & a & a^2 \\ 1 & b & b^2 \\ 1 & c & c^2 \end{vmatrix}

lines: Apply R₁ → R₁ − R₂ and R₂ → R₂ − R₃:

lines.text: \Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 0 & a-b & a^2-b^2 \\ 0 & b-c & b^2-c^2 \\ 1 & c & c^2 \end{vmatrix}

recall.must_convey: That R₁ → R₁ − R₂ and R₂ → R₂ − R₃ are applied, leaving two zeros in the first column.
accept: subtract the second row from the first and the third row from the second
apply R one minus R two and R two minus R three
row subtractions make the first column zero zero one
R one minus R two, R two minus R three cheyyali
take differences of neighbouring rows so a minus b appears

steps.why: Subtracting one row from another leaves the value of a determinant unchanged, and here it turns two of the three 1s in the first column into zeros.
common_mistakes: Expanding the determinant in full and hoping the algebra factorises.
Doing R₂ → R₂ − R₃ first, which changes R₂ before R₁ − R₂ uses it.

steps.label: Take (a−b) and (b−c) out
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Use a² − b² = (a−b)(a+b). Taking a factor out of a row divides that whole row by it, so both entries of R₁ change, not just the a² − b² entry.
steps.memory_tip: a² − b² = (a−b)(a+b), so (a−b) comes out of the whole first row.
lines: out of R₁ and (b−c) out of R₂:

recall.must_convey: That a²−b² and b²−c² are factorised so (a−b) leaves R₁ and (b−c) leaves R₂.
accept: a squared minus b squared is a minus b into a plus b so take a minus b out
take a minus b common from the first row and b minus c from the second
pull the two factors outside the determinant
a minus b ni first row nunchi common teesukovali
factorise the difference of squares and take the factor out of the row

steps.why: Taking a common factor out of a row multiplies the determinant by that factor outside, and this is where two of the three answer brackets come from.
common_mistakes: Taking (a−b) out of one entry only and leaving the rest of the row alone.

steps.label: Expand along the first column
steps.margin_note: Third mark. The first column is now (0, 0, 1), so only one term of the expansion survives. Its sign is (−1)³⁺¹ = +1, so nothing changes sign here.
steps.memory_tip: A column of (0, 0, 1) leaves exactly one term when you expand along it.
lines: Expand along C₁. Only the 1 in R₃ gives a

recall.must_convey: That the expansion is along C₁, that only the entry 1 in row 3 contributes, and that its sign is plus.
accept: expand along the first column since it is zero zero one
only the one in the third row gives a term and its sign is plus
the three by three drops to a two by two determinant
first column lo okate one undi kabatti oke term vasthundi
expand along the column with the zeros

steps.why: Expanding along the column that holds the zeros is what turns a 3×3 determinant into a single 2×2 one with no extra work.
common_mistakes: Expanding along the first row, which brings back all three terms.
Using a minus sign for the (3, 1) position, where the sign is plus.

steps.label: Reach (a−b)(b−c)(c−a)
steps.margin_note: Last mark. The 2×2 determinant is (b+c) − (a+b) = c − a, which is the third bracket. Check the letter order against what the question asks before boxing it.
steps.memory_tip: The 2×2 determinant gives (b+c) − (a+b) = c − a — the third bracket.

recall.must_convey: That the 2×2 determinant equals c − a, giving the product (a−b)(b−c)(c−a).
accept: b plus c minus a plus b is c minus a so the answer is the product of the three brackets
the last determinant gives c minus a
delta equals a minus b into b minus c into c minus a
chivari determinant c minus a isthundi
multiply the three factors to get the required result

steps.why: Each of the three brackets came from a different move: two from the row factors and this one from the 2×2 determinant. Together they are exactly the right-hand side asked for.
common_mistakes: Writing a − c instead of c − a, which flips the sign of the whole answer.
Leaving the answer as (a−b)(b−c) times a 2×2 determinant.
